title: In vivo recording and optotagging
objective: Explain how optotagging identifies a genetically defined neuron electrically.

steps.title: An electrode can't read genotype
steps.body: An in vivo electrode records spikes but can't tell which molecular type fired. **[[optotagging|Optotagging]]** solves this: express an opsin (e.g. ChR2) in one **[[Cre]]**-defined type, then flash light — neurons that fire *locked to the light* are that genetic type. You've tagged identity onto an electrical recording.

steps.prompt: In optotagging, which neurons are the tagged type?
options: Neurons that fire reliably, time-locked to each light flash
Neurons whose firing slowly ramps up over minutes of light
Neurons that fall silent during each of the light flashes
Neurons with the largest spikes once the light comes on
steps.explanation: Only opsin-expressing (Cre-defined) neurons fire right at the light pulse, so light-locked spikes reveal identity.

variants.setup: You flash light on ChR2-expressing, Cre-defined neurons during recording.
variants.prompt: How do you spot the tagged type?
options: Spikes that are tightly locked to the light pulses
Units whose firing creeps up seconds after light
Units that go quiet whenever the light is on
variants.reveal: Light-locked firing marks the opsin-expressing genetic type.

steps.setup: You want to know how one DRG subtype responds to colon distension in a living mouse.
options: Tag that subtype with an opsin, then read its spikes during distension
Record every unit during distension, then sort the subtype by spike shape
Dissociate the ganglion and culture all of its neurons in a dish first
steps.reveal: Optotagging lets you pick out one genetically defined subtype's activity in vivo during a real stimulus — connecting molecular identity to function in the behaving animal.

options: A genetic subtype to its own in vivo firing
A subtype's mRNA profile to its axon targets
A neuron's soma size to its firing threshold
variants.explanation: It assigns molecular identity to recorded activity in vivo.
